new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikoma is a privative tone language (H vs toneless, syllable = TBU) with no word-stress system: nouns may be entirely toneless or carry more than one H, so neither of the defining properties of stress (one obligatory, one culminative prominence per word) holds, and H placement is lexical (bisyllabic stems: toneless / penult-H / final-H), not weight- or edge-driven. Within the same ISO language, Nata is analysed as a stress-like system (exactly one H = most prominent syllable per word, lexically on sigma2 [retracted to a heavy initial syllable], sigma3 or the final syllable) and Isenye has obligatoriness only (H on stem-initial syllable or on all stem syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Aunio 2010 p. 7: in prepausal position 'the penultimate syllable is sometimes prominent', so final-H stems can surface with highest pitch on the penult; all such surface variants are optional free variation. Aunio 2013: final melodic H in verbs is retracted to a long-vowel (heavy) penult; optional Penultimate Shift in the Conditional. Aunio 2015 p. 6: Isenye may be moving toward regular penultimate stress under Swahili influence, but its mono- and trisyllabic nouns do not fit a penult pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on noun stems (domain = stem in Ikoma/Isenye, word in Nata) and melodic tone in inflected verbs; observations of penult prominence are for prepausal/isolation citation forms. No instrumental stress study exists.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog ikom1245 'Ikoma-Nata' (ISO ntk) lumps three varieties — Ikoma, Nata and Isenye/Ishenyi — which Aunio 2015 shows have 'fundamentally different lexical tonal systems': the quoted statement (no obligatoriness, no culminativity, lexical H placement) is for Ikoma proper (Aunio's Serengeti District data, also Higgins 2012 and Aunio 2010/2013); Nata is analysed as a stress-like system (one obligatory culminative H per word, position lexical: sigma2 retracted to heavy sigma1 / sigma3 / final; Anghelescu 2013, Aunio et al. 2019) and Isenye has obligatoriness only (stem-initial H or all-H). Glottolog 5.1 gives no separate codes for Nata or Isenye that I could verify; any catalog entry should be labelled 'Ikoma (variety of ikom1245)' and note the Nata/Isenye divergence.

sources.locator: Final discussion/comparison section, Helda author reprint p. 10 (pdf page 11; published pagination 359-371, approx. p. 368 — reprint warns pagination may differ); the Nata sentence quoted inside is from reprint p. 7 (section 'Nata')
sources.note: Whole paper evaluates the three varieties against Hyman's stress criteria: Ikoma nominal tone satisfies neither obligatoriness (toneless nouns exist) nor culminativity (multiply linked H), tones not weight-sensitive nor edge-aligned; Nata (after Anghelescu 2013) is 'a stress system where high tone represents the most prominent syllable', one obligatory H per word, lexically assigned to sigma2 (retracted to a heavy initial syllable), sigma3 or final; Isenye satisfies obligatoriness only (H stem-initial or all-H) and may be drifting toward regular penultimate stress under Swahili.

sources.note: Sect. 2.3 'Tone and syllable structure': Mara languages previously called accentual/'two type'; Ikoma has H vs toneless, toneless nouns and toneless verb forms, H attracted to heavy syllables, utterance-final H allowed; 'The Nata nominal tone system is a stress system in which every noun can have only one stressed syllable, realised as a H tone' (types: sigma2 unless initial heavy / sigma3 / final). Regular penultimate stress is reported only for some Zanaki speakers (not the target language).
